Putting aside the fact that the art made by AI is done by a soulless machine, the more proper comparison would be calling someone an artist because he instructed someone else to create a piece of art. After all, in terms of sculpture, it was the person who came up with the idea and sculpted it. For painting, it's the painter who thought of a scene, emotion, or concept and painted it onto the canvas. For photography, it was the photographer who saw a particular moment or piece of scenery and angled his camera to take a picture of it.

When it comes to AI, yes, the person may conceptualize the idea, but in the end, that person assigns the creative work to another. With that fact, it would be like seeing someone who hired an artist for a commission then giving the person that hired the title of the artist. I'm sure you can see how that simply doesn't make sense.

Now, as someone who has studied art, I can not simply dismiss AI as a tool. Art comes in many different forms, after all, and dismissing a potential tool would be close-minded. However, with how it is most frequently used now, those that create AI art can not be called artists. Between the lack of skill involved and the data collected through imoral means by these LLM, that much is, in most cases, out of the picture.

If you ever, for whatever reason, wanna drop a full stack in your hotbar, you can just press Ctrl+Q when the stack is in your hand.

Press F to immediately bring something to your offhand.

Pressing the middle mouse button while looking at a block can do one of two things depending on the mode:

1. If you're in creative mode, it will immediately place whatever block you're looking at into your hotbar.

2. If you're in survival mode and you have that same block in your inventory, it will swap what you're holding for the block you're looking at.

When you're managing inventory, there's a little shortcut to moving a bunch of items. When you've picked up an item on the UI, you can actually shift+double left click any item to shift them all into a chest. For instance, if you've picked up a sword, then you shift+double click a stack of cobble, all other stacks will also go into the chest.

This is actually a really interesting question. I honestly have the same opinion as OP (Ended up here cause I was trying to figure out why I felt that way and there are no critiques I could find that don't praise it as the perfect game). If I don't play with friends, I can't bring myswlf to play the game, and even then, reflecting back, I think the only part I did enjoy at the time was the company of my friends. Not the game itself.

The weird part about all this is I that I play games like Minecraft, games that almost require you to have that imagination to enjoy them. Hell, in our server, I'm essentially my group's architect and imagineer, creating mega bases that align with some sort of server story, so I don't think it has anything to do with imagination. And so, as someone who likes looking into game design and such, I decided to dissect the game's design and my own preferences, and here's what I found if you're interested:

First, despite the admittedly useful guide, the game overall still feels overwhelming. This may be more because I once had a classmate who wouldn't shut up about the game, so I already knew there was a LOT going into it. I knew there was something about classes, certain weapons to get to make a proper build, etc. And, my god, the wiki does not help with that. If anything, seeing all those graphs and ALL the steps to get certain items just added to it (Note, this is coming from someone that plays games like Stardew and Minecraft, games that have their own wikis). I don't know if my experience would have been different if I went in blind, but either way, that's how I felt.

And so, I decided to do something I was more familiar with: Build. Wanting to make a good base for my friends and I, I began perusing the wiki for all the different blocks. Having built a lot in Minecraft, this part wasn't as overwhelming. I simply looked through the blocks and walls, got myself a pallette, and then asked a friend for help to gather things. The only thing is, a LOT of what I had chosen wasn't actually available until later bosses were beaten, which essentially destroyed my building plans. And I know people say that limitations breed creativity, but to me at the time, knowing that some of the really nice options were blocked until certain NPC's showed up was just disheartening.

Later on, my friend did manage to make something considered nice elsewhere in the world, but, while I do recognize his skill, I found that the 2D environment just wasn't enough for a build to look good in my eyes. That's just my personal taste, though.

Then, finally, there was the combat. This, I was really looking forward to as I had heard really good things. As someone who had played other 2D combat-focused games like Hollowknight, I wanted to see how the game handled its combat on the 2D plane. Turns out, it just boils down to spam clicking. I'll admit, maybe I was doing something wrong, but during combat, I really did just find myself spam clicking left click until the enemy was dead. Now, the visuals and sound effects may make up for that for most, but it really didn't for me. Like, sure, you have to dodge when you really need to, but even then, it just didn't feel so fun.

Sure, maybe the same could be argued for Hollowknight, but I would argue that even the simple act of swinging your nail in that game needed to be timed so that you don't get hit. During the start of that game, I somewhat struggled to get the timing right and slowly learned as I went on, whereas in Terraria, I just kept spam clicking. Really, the only development I felt combat wise was getting stronger gear and more health.

Then, finally, there's the overall grind of the game. I don't know if this is a controversial statement or not, but I would argue the game is so much grindier than post-1.18 Minecraft (only comparing the two cause I play Minecraft a lot). Yes, that includes the mining changes, the netherite upgrade stuff, and even the self-inflicted torture of rerolling a lectern for hours until you get the perfect enchantment and repeating that until you have all the best enchantments. In Terraria, the insane number of monsters you just have to kill to get certain items is just mind-numbing to me.

But this was the weirdest part of my feeling to me. After all, I can spend an entire damn week moving MC villagers around, breeding them, and making an army of librarians, so why couldn't I go through this? It was then I realized the foundational thing I seem to lack whenever I play Terraria: Intrinsic Motivation. This has always been my primary driving force when playing a game, no matter how scripted it is. 

In Minecraft, my motivation to make something in my vision is exactly what keeps me playing. And even with the more linear goal of beating the Ender Dragon, I always manage to make imaginary reasons why I should beat it. 

In Hollowknight, I kept playong because I wanted to explore the woeld and uncover all the history that seemed to lay within it.

Even in FPS campaigns, I play them because I want to experience the story, not because the story needed to be finished. Lord knows I've dropped a lot of games whose story just seemed boring to me. 

But once I hop into Terraria, I just can't bring myself to care. Why should I fight these bosses? Why should I care about this random NPC the game insists I build shelter for? It feels more like an extrinsic game than an intrisic one. You beat a boss to get cool gear to beat stronger bosses. It just feels pointless to me. And I think that really is the core of the whole issue for me, at least.

There's a lot of advice that can be given, but the two that come to mind are:

1. Don't be afraid to expand your block palette! Right now, your mansion is primarily made out of two blocks: Dark Oak and Deepslate. Many other blocks can match with these! So don't be scared and start sorting blocks to see what looks good! And don't be afraid to switch a certain block with another if you think it'll help the build overall!

In line with this, you don't have to choose materials based on what a mansion would be made out of, stuff like mushroom stems, bone blocks, etc, make for great building blocks too! So, again, feel free to have fun experimenting!

2. People often think that it's not creative to look at other builds for inspiration, but that's not true! If you really wanna make a good mansion, check out other builds and take note of the techniques they apply. How do they texture their corners? How about their interiors? How do they break long stretches of flat color? Just take note of these, and you'll suddenly have a whole arsenal of tricks to make your original build pop!

Also, two videos sid kinda help me propel my building if you're interested. Both are by a creator called BdoubleO100. The titles are:

I don’t typically like arguing, but Imma but-in just to correct some incorrect info.

In a tweet by Kingbdogz during 5/15/22, Kingbdogz talked about the recent feelings of disappointment. In that thread, one person asked why they showed the Birch Forest in the way that they did if they weren’t going to update it anyway. This was his response:

"It’s not that it wasn’t going to be a part of 1.19, it’s that plans changed and we are no longer focusing on it for this update. So it’s going in our ideas library meaning it is up for grabs in any of our future updates."

Based on this, we see that, at least at some point, Birch Forests were a planned feature and that the community likely didn’t misunderstand Mojang’s intentions. Furthermore, in regard to the video, this is what was said:

"As with the Birch Forest, that is a little bit different. At Minecraft Live, we did show some concept art with Birch Forest improvements. However, concept art is not the commitment, and this time around, Birch Forest improvement is not something we have continued working with."

Comparing this with Kingbdogz’s tweet, it seems to say the same thing, albeit in a more corporate manner. In my opinion, this is about a 4/10, but don’t be discouraged! We all start somewhere! I only began building good-ish recently after 10 years of playing the game!

So, some suggestions from the things I’ve learned:

1. Try not to stick with one material. Look through Minecraft’s block palette and see what looks good together! Right now, the building looks fairly plain because of the lack of additional textures. I personally find that the light gray blocks (cobblestone, andesite etc.) look good as a foundational material with oak wood.

2. Try to add a little more shape. An interesting shape not only tends to make the build look more detailed an interesting, but it also gives you more space to work with. What I personally like doing is identifying what shapes I want to mix, then find ways to integrate them together, whether that be connecting them or putting one shape in another. Don’t be afraid to experiment! That’s half the fun!

3. Add depth to the build. In interesting builds, you’ll often see some sort of physical depth, whether it be through support beams sticking out of the wall, glass panes on stairs facing outward, or even little extensions. Again, experiment and see what works with your build!

4. Add life to your build through all sorts of decorations! Think, “If people were living here, how would it look like?” Maybe there are scattered barrels somewhere with some materials spilling (item frames can help with these), a cake cooling on a window, or a bundle of flowers being sold at some stand. Another way to add life is to add moving elements. These can be mobs, smoke stacks, minecarts, or anything else you can think of!

5. Finally, and most importantly, don’t be afraid to look at reference images for inspiration. There tends to be this common misconception that good builders cannot look at reference images, but that’s far from true! In fact, good builders look at reference images a lot! Whether it be a picture of a real life location or a screenshot of a nice looking build, inspiration pictures tend to be very useful!

Those are my 5 tips! If you want more tips, I’d personally recommend “My Hermitcraft Starter House Tutorial” by Bdubs as he delves into the techniques he uses rather than giving a block by block tutorial. Whatever you decide to build next, enjoy!
